::: {#exm-rejection-counts}
#### Outcome counts in a simulated family of 1000 tests

With real data the truth is unknown, so $V$ and $S$ cannot be counted.
A simulation knows the truth.
Simulate $m = 1000$ z-tests,
of which $m_0 = 900$ have a true null hypothesis
(a standard Gaussian statistic $Z_j$)
and 100 have a false one
(a Gaussian statistic with mean 3 and variance 1).
Each p-value is $2 \normcdf(-\abs{z_j})$.
Rejecting every null hypothesis with $p_j \le 0.05$ gives the counts of @def-rejection-counts:

```{r}
#| label: rejection-counts
#| code-fold: false
simulate_tests <- function(m = 1000, m0 = 900, shift = 3) {
  is_null <- rep(c(TRUE, FALSE), c(m0, m - m0))
  z <- rnorm(m, mean = ifelse(is_null, 0, shift))
  list(p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(z)), is_null = is_null)
}
count_outcomes <- function(reject, is_null) {
  c(
    U = sum(!reject & is_null), V = sum(reject & is_null),
    T = sum(!reject & !is_null), S = sum(reject & !is_null)
  )
}

set.seed(571)
sim <- simulate_tests()
counts <- count_outcomes(sim$p <= 0.05, sim$is_null)
matrix(
  counts[c("U", "V", "T", "S")],
  nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(
    c("Null true", "Null false"),
    c("Not rejected", "Rejected")
  )
) |>
  as.table() |>
  addmargins()
```

The procedure made $R =$ `r counts[["V"]] + counts[["S"]]` rejections,
of which $V =$ `r counts[["V"]]` were false positives.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#rem-counts-unobserved}
#### Only the number of rejections is observed

$V$, $S$, $U$, $T$ and $R$ are random,
because they depend on the data.
In practice only $m$ and $R$ are observed;
$m_0$ and the split of $R$ into $V$ and $S$ are not.
Error rates are therefore defined as properties of a procedure over repeated data sets,
not of the particular list of rejections that one data set produces.
:::
